description.de:
The Danube Floodplain National Park in Austria (Nationalpark Donau-Auen) protects one of the last remaining 
floodplain landscapes in Europe. It harbors a variety of habitats and is divided by a flood protection dam. The 
aim of this study was to assess the diversity of earthworms that inhabit the National Park and its unique habitats. 
We investigated 15 habitat types attributed to 5 general categories: forests, grasslands, riverine sites, arable sites 
and shrublands. Earthworms were sampled from soil by a combination of handsorting and mustard extraction, 
and from dead wood of selected forest types. We recorded 23 of the roughly 60 earthworm species known from 
Austria, including the first Austrian record of Helodrilus serbicus, rediscovery of Dendrobaena steineri, thirty years 
after first and only record, and regionally endemic Vindoboscolex hrabei. In soils, species richness was the highest 
in forest sites (median of 3), with flooded forests showing the highest species richness (median of 7). Earthworm 
abundance and species richness in soil seemed unaffected by the dam. In contrast, dead wood in repeatedly 
flooded areas showed higher earthworm density and species richness, suggesting an influence of the dam-altered 
flooding regime. Earthworm community composition also differed markedly between forest soils and adjacent 
dead wood. Among all habitat types, dead wood and riverine sites harboured the most distinct assemblages, 
dominated by specialist species. These findings underscore the importance of floodplain forests and their unique 
microhabitats for earthworm diversity and indicate that flood-regulating structures can shape earthworm 
communities in soils and dead wood.

title.de: Across the river and into the trees: Earthworms in a Central European  Floodplain National Park
